restatements.text: Provides the title of the act.
Declares findings regarding taxation, program efficiency, and the need to apply the state spending limit to new taxes.
States the act's purpose is to require audits of programs receiving new special taxes and to prohibit new taxes from being exempt from the state spending limit.

Requires the State Auditor to prepare a pre-election financial and performance audit for programs that would receive money from a proposed special tax initiative, mandates the inclusion of its executive summary in the voter information guide, and requires reimbursement from the tax revenue if the measure passes.

Requires the State Auditor to conduct ongoing financial and performance audits every four years for programs funded by special taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026, with costs reimbursed from the tax revenue.
Prohibits any state tax enacted on or after January 1, 2026, from being exempted from the Government Spending Limitation, and voids the collection of any tax that includes such an exemption.
Defines key terms used in the article, including the Government Spending Limitation and special taxes.
Applies the new requirements to all statewide initiatives submitted to voters on or after January 1, 2026.
Declares that this measure prevails over and voids any conflicting initiative on the same ballot that imposes different audit rules or includes a tax exempt from the spending limit.
Ensures that if any part of the act is found invalid, the remaining parts stay in effect.
Sets the effective and operative date of the act.
Requires the act to be liberally construed to achieve its intent.

Requires the Attorney General to appoint an independent counsel to defend the act if the Governor and Attorney General refuse to do so, and establishes a continuous appropriation from the General Fund to cover the legal costs.

analysis.answer: Current law was not provided. The measure requires the State Auditor to conduct automatic pre-election and ongoing four-year performance and financial audits of all programs receiving money from new or increased special taxes. It also strictly prohibits any new state tax enacted after January 1, 2026, from being exempted from the existing Government Spending Limitation.

Direct costs include the expense of conducting detailed pre-election and ongoing audits by the State Auditor, which the measure states must be paid from the revenues generated by the special taxes if they pass. There are also potential costs to the General Fund from the continuous appropriation created to pay independent counsel to defend the measure if state officials decline to do so.

Taxpayers funding special taxes ultimately bear the cost of the mandated audits, as those costs are subtracted from the tax revenues. Special interest groups and lawmakers seeking to pass new special taxes face the added hurdle of pre-election audits and the prohibition on exempting their proposals from the constitutional spending limit. Taxpayers may broadly benefit from increased transparency and the stricter enforcement of overall spending caps.

Proponents of new taxes may try to structure them as general taxes or use alternative funding mechanisms to avoid the mandatory special-tax audits. The Legislature may face stricter overall limits on total appropriations, as new special taxes cannot be exempted from the Gann Limit, potentially forcing cuts elsewhere or resulting in tax rebates if the total limit is exceeded. State agencies may alter their operations and record-keeping in anticipation of facing regular performance audits and having to demonstrate plans for 10% budgetary savings.

The measure asserts that state programs are inefficient, waste taxpayer dollars, and avoid the discipline of the state spending limit through exemptions. It addresses these problems by legally requiring the State Auditor to publish pre-election and ongoing performance audits for new special taxes, thereby providing voters and policymakers with data. It also closes the exemption loophole, forcing all new state taxes to compete within the existing constitutional spending cap.

The California State Auditor gains significant discretion and authority to evaluate special tax programs and issue mandated recommendations for budget savings. An independent counsel could gain considerable legal authority to defend the measure if the Attorney General and Governor decline to do so.

Administrative costs are explicitly embedded in the measure, which requires that the State Auditor's expenses for conducting extensive audits be reimbursed from the revenue generated by the special taxes, thereby reducing the funds that actually reach the programs the taxes were designed to support.
Because it adds an article to the California Constitution, its core provisions can only be undone or modified by another voter-approved constitutional amendment.
